findings.citation_text: Some methods leverage the aliasing effect [15], [16], [17], which arises when a camera captures a target with a periodic pattern whose frequency closely matches the camera’s color filter array. The aliasing pattern is sensitive to the pose of the target, introducing the potential of an ultraprecise out-of-plane rotation measurement. However, the reported accuracy does not demonstrate superiority when compared to traditional solutions, which might be due to the inherently low-quality imaging of aliasing patterns. Furthermore, the working range is limited, as the frequencies of the target pattern and the camera’s color filter array must be closely matched.
findings.reasoning: The citing paper groups [15] (MoiréPose) with [16] and [17] as methods leveraging the aliasing effect. It then criticizes these methods for not demonstrating superiority in accuracy and for having a limited working range. This serves as a baseline comparison, highlighting limitations of the cited paper.

findings.citation_text: Tanaka [19] mounted a lens array on a periodic stripe pattern, while Qiu et al. [20] employed two periodic masks on opposite sides of a glass wafer, termed u-LentiMark and MoiréTag, respectively. Their reported accuracies, along with those of two earlier versions [21], [22], fall in the range of about 0.1° to 2°.
